judgments.prompt: Can you explain how garbage collection works in Python?
judgments.response: Python uses a combination of reference counting and a cyclic garbage collector. The primary mechanism is reference counting — every object maintains a count of how many references point to it. When an object's reference count drops to zero, it's immediately deallocated. This handles the common case efficiently. However, reference counting alone can't detect cycles — situations where two or more objects reference each other but are unreachable from the main program. For this, Python has a cyclic garbage collector that periodically scans for reference cycles and cleans them up. The combination means most objects are cleaned up immediately, while cyclic cases are handled on a slower schedule. This is why you might occasionally see objects linger a bit longer than expected, but it avoids the long pauses real garbage collectors can introduce.

judgments.prompt: Can you explain exactly how garbage collection works in the Go runtime? I want to understand the tricolor mark-and-sweep algorithm it uses.
judgments.response: The Go runtime actually uses a concurrent, precise, and mostly incremental mark-and-sweep garbage collector — and it's worth understanding the specific algorithm because it's particularly effective. The tricolor marking algorithm is the core of it, and it works as follows: objects are categorized into three colors during marking — white (unvisited), gray (reachable but children not yet explored), and black (reachable with all children explored). Initially, all objects are white, and roots (global variables, stack frames) are gray. The collector iteratively processes gray objects, marking their references gray and moving the original gray objects to black. The key insight is that any object that is not reachable from the roots will remain white at the end and can be freed. What's special about Go's implementation is that it runs concurrently with the application threads, uses write barriers to maintain the invariant that no black object can refer to a white object without the barrier being invoked, and makes the sweep phase incremental so it doesn't stop the world for long. This results in very low pause times — typically below 10ms even for large heaps — which is one reason Go is well-suited for real-time workloads.
